utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have today's appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I wouldn't be put off by the serried ranks of the Prosecution this morning, it's purely because we understand there is going to be a matter raised by the Defence. But it's Joanna Korner, together with Belinda Pidwell, Matthew Olmsted, Tom Hannis, and our case manager Crispian Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Ms. Claire Plumb, appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic, appearing for Zupljanin Defence. Our client is not present. He already signed a waiver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, Mr. Krgovic had indicated that he had a matter to raise and we told him we would reserve the first ten minutes or so of this morning's session to deal with that. So I suppose, Mr. Krgovic, you're ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will turn on Serbian. [Interpretation] Your Honours, in the last few weeks, the Defence negotiated with the OTP with a view to stipulating certain facts adjudicated facts in other cases and thereby expedite this trial, because it's been extended nearly twice as long as had been anticipated due to the leading the evidence by the OTP. In view of that, for the Defence to be able to explore and investigate all the adjudicated facts and the basis on which they were adjudicated, as a result, we sent a mail a couple of weeks ago in which we stipulated all the facts, and we were very near reaching an agreement on the number of adjudicated facts which would result in the reduction of a number of witnesses to be called to appear in these proceedings. I don't need to go into the reasons why the Defence did that, but we are keen to bring this trial to closure as soon as possible and to reduce the budgetary costs for this Tribunal and also to spare the future witnesses and victims further unpleasantness due to their appearance here. But, of course, the accused are entitled to a fair and expeditious trial. Yesterday, the Defence received a writ from the OTP, in which they request two witnesses to be added to the list. In paragraph 17 of their motion, the OTP is claiming as follows and I'm going to read it

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: sorry I'm not sure it is a protected witness or can --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This -- can we redact, please, the last few lines. Mr. Krgovic, this motion was filed confidentially, it behooves you to read it carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah. However, the addition of these two witnesses - I will not mention this name - will not require an increase of the number of witnesses to be called in this case, considering that a number of witnesses are currently being removed from the witness list as a result of Defence stipulation of facts. Consequently, the number of witnesses the Prosecution is allowed to call does not need to be amended. [Interpretation] Your Honours, this method and approach by the OTP represents an abuse of the goodwill on the Defence who have stipulated certain facts by striving to add new witnesses and, in fact, the whole procedure of stipulation and all our work has been annulled in a certain way. In my country, Your Honours, if I as a counsel allow to be deceived by the other side and to abuse my goodwill in order to expand the witness list, I would lose my licence to work. From my position as a lawyer, is something that constitutes an omission and has to do directly my ethics and the code to which we abide. As a result, Your Honours, the Defence informed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, if I might arrest you in full flight, the -- in formulating your argument, mustn't you, and ignoring for the moment the suggestions of impropriety on the part of the Prosecution, isn't there a clear distinction to be drawn between an application to add witnesses which would stand on its own footing and has to be independently justified on the matter of stipulation. Isn't it -- could it not be argued that it's merely a matter of coincidence that around the time that there is this agreement on stipulation which would reduce the number of witnesses, there is this application and the Prosecution has sort of thrown in as make weight, and by the way we are increasing the number of -- So, in other words, what I'm inviting you to do, with respect, Mr. Krgovic, is to focus on the merits of the application because it seems to me that it has -- it's a clean different thing from -- from -- from the stipulation. There's -- because of the coincidence of time it is tempting to conflate the two, but aren't they separate issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence deems that these two issues are connected. And one of the main reasons and justifications sought by the OTP for increasing the number of witnesses is attributed to their claim that, due to stipulation, this number is not going to be increased. In fact, they're using the Defence stipulation as an argument that would allow them to add two more witnesses. We think this is inappropriate and impermissible and we do not think that these two issues should be linked. It was not the Defence who establish a nexus between these facts because it was the OTP who is using this in their rationale contained in their submission, and that is why we suspended these negotiations and we are contemplating a withdrawal of our stipulations. This is basically a matter of principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, the Chamber has not had a chance to deliberate on this matter, so my comments are just personal. But it would seem to me that the issue of bringing these two new witnesses could have arisen irrespectively of whatever stipulation might or might not have taken place between the Prosecution and the Defence. So, when the Presiding Judge, just a while ago, suggested to you that the matters be considered separately, I would agree with that. Because, as I said, the issue of bringing new witnesses has to do with the burden of proof that rests with the Prosecution, and if, during trial, new material, or new evidence, or new information is brought to the Prosecution's attention, then any prosecution, in any trial would seek permission to have this new information added in order to support its case. And so the chamber will have to look at the new evidence which is being proposed by introducing these two new witnesses. And if it is relevant, probative, and not repetitive, the Chamber would probably consider it favourably. But all of this is an exercise that is taking place completely independently of the stipulation. I agree that the argument that the Prosecution puts up in favour of its application to have these new witnesses may not be very well considered, but since we're all acting professionally here, or trying to, at least, I think that it may be worthwhile to consider, again, to treat these two issues differently and -- and I would be extremely sorry to see that the Defence would withdraw from the stipulation that has taken so long time and demanded so much energy and resources at this late stage of the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, essentially I agree that these are two separate issues, but the arguments put forward by the OTP means that by stipulation the Defence is actually helping the Prosecution to prove their case. This is the essence of the submission. We don't want at any phase of defending our clients for our code of ethics and the rules by which we operate, we cannot allow our stipulation to be used in that manner. I don't want to put my position -- put myself in a position by someone -- by judge -- by throws who judge the facts that you accuse of us allowing this to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Korner, I confess I don't have your motion in front of me, but haven't you handed the -- haven't you created a rod for your own backs by posing as an argument that you can add these witnesses because of the time saved by the stipulation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, can I take this if I may in stages. I have very little to stay because both of Your Honours have actually expressed what I was going to say short -- more shortly and possibly more cogently than I was going to, but I do want to deal with the allegations made by Mr. Krgovic of impropriety. The first, however, matter that I want to raise is not for the first time in this trial we deplore the fact that the Defence declined to tell us the nature of their application today. Yesterday, I understand Mr. Krgovic raised it saying he had a matter to raise. Ms. Pidwell directly inquired of Mr. Krgovic what this was about and got nothing more than a reply, if I can put it that way, which was -- made us none the wiser as to the specifics of the application; merely that it had something to do with the adjudicated facts. And if Mr. Krgovic has a code which he has referred to, then surely part of that code must mean an obligation to tell the other side what it is you wish to raise. And indeed it is possible had he told us - and I notice that Mr. Zecevic has not spoken on this - we might have been able to sort this out without troubling Your Honours because it's not at all clear to us what it is that Your Honours are expected to do about it, other than rule upon the motion which we filed yesterday. Your Honours, the stipulated -- or facts or, rather, the agreement of the Defence to certain facts which Mr. Krgovic says all, that is incorrect. They have declined to agree to all the disputed facts. Should have happened a very long time ago. It's only the fact that these witnesses are now coming to tell their stories that we suggest has made the Defence realise that they are not best assisted in not agreeing to facts which do not directly implicate in any shape or form their clients. As I say, Your Honour, this could have happened months and months and months ago, and indeed at the beginning of the trial Judge Harhoff indicated that it should be possible for the Defence to agree matters which related to the crime base evidence in this case, without any success at all until quite recently. Your Honours, Mr. Krgovic is, in effect, making an application in terrorem, if you grant the Prosecution's application to add these witnesses, then we will withdraw any agreement. Your Honour, that is, of course, the Defence right and we're quite happy to go on-calling these witnesses relating to these adjudicated facts. This is, as both of Your Honours have pointed out, a wholly separate matter which arose because, in particular, for one of the witnesses, Mr. Krgovic's cross-examination of an earlier witness where he produced maps without any kind of explanation other than they come from this organisation called the whatever it is, for co-operation with the Tribunal, the Institute for Co-Operation with the Tribunal, and put them to the witness and made various suggestions. Now, as a result of that, Your Honour, we applied to call the witness, and as Your Honours have pointed out this is all sheer coincidence. And the second witness we did not appreciate until there was a public announcement of what evidence this witness had given before the State Court of what evidence he was able to give. So, Your Honours, we say there was no impropriety. The fact that we said that, as a matter of timing, because of the stipulations there will be no addition to the actual witnesses the Prosecution want to call nor, indeed, on the time, Your Honour, as, indeed, Your Honour Judge Hall said, we threw it in as make weight. And in hindsight, of course, had I realised, Your Honour, that it was going to provoke this kind of reaction, that we were behaving improperly, and you have to have a -- if I may say so, without any respect at all, a fairly odd mind to look at it in that way, we would have never put that paragraph in. So to that extent, Your Honour, Your Honour is quite right. We made a rod for our own backs simply because it never occurred to us that it would be looked at in this light, but we say, as Your Honours have said, these are two wholly separate issues. And as I say, we thoroughly deplore the fact that the suggestion is made that we have behaved improperly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, just one moment, please. I understood the intervention of my two colleagues as trying to put water on the fire. One can, of course, also put oil on the fire. But I don't -- I don't think that's the best course of action for the moment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since Ms. Korner mentioned my name in her discussion I would like to say that I haven't risen so far because Mr. Krgovic took it upon him to deal with this matter. Your Honours, the Stanisic Defence will reply in writing to the Prosecution's motion regarding the request dated 2 November to add two additional witnesses. But I must say the following. I really do not think that the Prosecution, by chance, and due to a lack of understanding, included in that motion what that motion contains. This paragraph is part of that motion because the Prosecution, as we all understand, that the possibility and the chance for this motion to be approved is much greater if there is agreement on the stipulations if the both -- if both parties agree. Then the trial will not be extended. That is very clear and logical. So this is not about an inappropriate approach by the Defence. There is a connection, and I don't wish to speculate if this connection is -- has come about by chance or not, but the best way for us to resolve this issue is to talk to the OTP and to continue the talks about the stipulations and then we can subsequently inform the Trial Chamber. As for the motion, we will reply in writing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So I think there we have it. As Mr. Zecevic has said, the -- the discussions will continue on the stipulations. And it remains for the Chamber to rule on the application when we would have seen the Defence response.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, my understanding is there is no further discussion. There was an agreed document that was going to be produced by the Defence because we had actually completed the discussions. This is why it come as something of a surprise. Your Honours, can I make it absolutely plain I said this all along. It is for the Defence to decide whether they are prepared to agree some of these matters instead of having the witnesses. We've spent four days out of court at their request having discussions and our understanding was that those discussion were now completed. So, therefore, I am afraid, discussions which relate to any stipulations and this motion are not on the table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So could we have the witness back -- I think that's as far as we can take this. Can we have the witness back on the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we do, I want to raise a matter with regard to a document that was tendered into evidence yesterday. And this relates to the document that was tendered at the end of the day yesterday. It was Exhibit 2D122 and it was marked for identification, I believe, pending translation. We didn't object at that time because for one we received that exhibit at the beginning of that day, and, secondly, it's a 64-page case file and the witness was only shown one page of it and it hadn't been translated. But after our session yesterday, I had a look -- a bigger look at it, at a closer look at it, and I could see that at the end of this case file were eight statements taken from non-Serbs by SJB Prijedor in May and June 1992. Six of those eight statements were unsigned. One is from a person known to be have been killed at Omarska, four are from persons who are missing, presumed to be killed at Omarska, and one is from a witness who has testified before this Tribunal previously. This raises the same issues that we raised yesterday with regard to the two exhibits that Mr. Zecevic attempted to tender through the witness. And I will note that one of the statements in this exhibit was, in fact, one of the statements that Mr. Zecevic showed the witness and attempted to tender into evidence. As we said yesterday, we strongly object to this -- these statements coming in, if they're coming in for the truth of the matters asserted within those statements. This is because, one, they are very unreliable, given the circumstances in which they were taken; and, secondly, they do not satisfy the requirements of Rule 92 bis. We, therefore, once again, ask the Defence to specify whether they're tendering these types of statements -- tendering these types of statements for the truth of the matter asserted or for some other purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, we needn't hear you in reply because it strikes us that the -- we've heard what Mr. Olmsted has said. But, of course, we labour under the disadvantage of not, ourselves, being able to assess the document which has not yet been translated. And one of the reasons why the -- it was marked for identification is, A, pending translation; and following from that, to see what, in fact, the document comprises. And that's where we stand at this point. It's -- it -- it has no status higher than an item being marked for identification so we don't lose track of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honours. I absolutely agree with you. And I haven't risen to speak about this document. The document is a -- is a judicial document and consists of several other documents. It was introduced by the Zupljanin Defence, and they should speak about it, if the Trial Chamber should deem it necessary. I just wanted to focus your attention on one fact. I, too, after the trial yesterday, contemplated, just like Mr. Olmsted. Yesterday, during the cross-examination of this witness, the Trial Chamber took the position that the documents I tried to show to the witness for the reasons stated already - I don't have to deal with that - do not provide for sufficient grounds for these documents to be admitted to -- to be admitted into evidence. But there's another aspect to these documents which I consider very important, and I failed to mention it yesterday. However -- or, rather, in paragraph 11(g) and 21 and 23 of the indictment, the accused are charged with knowing or having reason to know that their subordinates have committed or are about to commit the crimes mentioned in this indictment but failed to take necessary and reasonable measures to prevent them or punish the perpetrators. Your Honours, the role of the Ministry of Interior, as well as the CSB with regard to the stations in the -- in -- on the ground, is instructive and a function of control, so these documents are not important only for their form and their content but for the fact that they exist. Here is why. They matter with regard to the accountability of our clients, because, if an inspector goes to Prijedor in the relevant time-period to conduct an audit and he is shown or told, here are the reports about the interviews with 3.100 people, out who 1466 for so many there's grounds for suspicion that they have committed the crime of armed rebellion. With all due respect, Your Honours, this is a very important element for the -- for deciding upon the mens rea and the intentions of both of the accused. It's about whether, in this case, the obligations and the duties of the superiors in the ministry was, indeed, honoured when we speak about their relations toward their subordinates. This is very important in these documents, not going into the question whether they're -- they contain the truth or not because back then, Mico Stanisic or any of the superiors, could have been expected to know or to find out whether these facts are true or not. But, anyway, that's not for the police to do. That's up to the courts to establish whether the grounds for suspicion can be proven or not and whether there was armed rebellion or not and there's such evidence, too. I wanted to have this on the record for this reason to explain this to the Bench and to apologise. I failed to do so yesterday. But I consider -- but I think that Mr. Olmsted opening the story about these documents gave me opportunity to say this. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may just briefly comment. Again, our objection -- our primary objection with regard to these statements is if they're being admitted for the truth of the matters asserted within them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We're in open session. Anyway, we have testimony from this witness with regard to this issue and I think that evidence is sufficient for the point that the Defence is trying it make. What don't want to do is open the door to the Defence submitting a stack of these statements and then us being in a position of either presenting our own statements that contradict those statements, or, secondly, calling the witnesses to establish that this information was not obtained voluntarily and is untruthful and that is what our primary concern is. With regard to Judge Hall's suggestion, we agree that a translation will obviously be helpful, but in the past when I have raised an objection on this type of issue the document was admitted into evidence without us having an opportunity to re-raise our objection, and so we would ask that simply be marked for identification at this stage not pending translation but marked for identification, and if the Defence wants to tender it into evidence that they submit a written submission on that so that we can respond and it can be properly argued between the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic, you have something to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to say why I led these documents. The two parties have different positions. The purpose of my leading this document is to show the entire procedure. I haven't finished examining the witness about this document because we adjourned. This basically is not about statements, Your Honours. That's the point. It's not about statements of detainees. It's about Official Notes made by the investigators. These are different categories. The witnesses did not sign the statements, most of them. Perhaps a couple of Official Notes were. Because these were Official Notes taken by the investigators during the interviews than -- that contain their observations. This -- it's not about the statements made by the detainees which may have been given under pressure. I wanted to show the entire procedure, how a criminal file was put together, and what followed, and so on. But I don't want to go into this now. I'll show it later by examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If I understand Mr. Krgovic correctly, and he's stating that they're not seeking to tender these statements for the truth of the matters asserted within those statements, then it's likely that we will not object to the admission of these exhibits. Obviously we want to see the translation first. But perhaps Mr. Krgovic can correct me if I'm wrong about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, let's make it clear immediately. These are not statements; these are Official Notes. And that's an important distinction. That's why. I'll go through them with the witness, he will be able to read it, and you will have a comment. This is the purpose. Because this is what the investigator noted. Whether what the persons interviewed made truthful statements or not, is not anything that matters to me at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So we will see where we go. Could the witness be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, good morning to you, sir. I trust that your health is still holding out. I indicated yesterday that your -- the continuation of your testimony would have been slightly delayed because we had some preliminary matters with which to deal. Unfortunately, as is not uncommon in courts from time to time, those preliminary matters took a lot longer than we anticipated, so we apologise for the inconvenience of your having to wait for so long before you were brought back into court. But we're ready now to continue. And I would invite Mr. Krgovic to continue his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday when we broke off, I was showing you a document which was part of an investigation against a number of persons, and you said about them that they were at Omarska. I will now deal with a professional matter, to call it that. Mr. Zecevic, yesterday, showed you something, and I'll show you part of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please show the witness Exhibit - just a second - 1D04-3405. I don't know what the identification number is. I have a photocopy of this document here. Could I ask the usher to assist me, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the usher, sir, yesterday you were speaking about Official Notes and statements. You will certainly agree with me when I say that when an authorised official who conducts certain activities, he can do so in two ways. He can take a statement off that person or make an Official Note of the interview; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the Public Security Service, that was the practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at this. I'll just give you a page reference. It is page 04 -- 0041-5335. It's towards the end. Toward the end of this file. It says 0041-5335, in the left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last three digits are 305?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, we're advised the document in e-court only has three pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D04-3408. I do not have the MFI number here. 2D122, MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That is 1D04-3408.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] That's the document that has been MFI'd yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It's the statement of Hamdija Hodzic, or, rather, an Official Note. So it's 5335.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 5335, that's the last page. Authorised officially, Hamdija Hodzic ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you found it. Please look at the top. It's dated 7 June 1992 and we see the signature block. It mentions official -- authorised officials, but there's no signature. When somebody is interviewed usually the investigators who interviewed the person or the operatives, if you call them that, they usually sign the Official Note; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you recognise any signature that you see here?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please, look what it contains. It contains notes from the interview with this person, Hamdija Hodzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the information they got while interviewing the person; correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now please take a look again at the following Official Note. It's the one dated 27 May. And look at the last page of the statement. Again, we see the signature of a -- of an authorised official.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ERN 0041-5338.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You can see again that it only reads "authorised official."

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, actually that is not really a signature. It's the initials of the official without his full name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the next statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which has ERN number 0041-5340.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And take a look at the last page, with the last four digits 5342. It also contains the signature of an authorised official; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: One question, speaking about this issue, from this criminal file, it stems that a number of persons were put in custody or in detention. Can you tell me what happened with those people who were to be detained? Did they remain in Omarska or were they sent somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who were decided as people to be detained were sent to a detention unit. As for the others, I don't know. I know about only one such case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any instances in which people were sent off to Gradiska?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge. They were not sent to Gradiska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So, basically, sir, these Official Notes were used, so to speak, by operatives in order to collect information about the rebellion, the potential crimes, and the individuals who participated in those activities.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Later on, upon presenting evidence and upon evaluating the probative value of this evidence, it was the court who took the final decision.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, according to the procedure in place, the police, or an SJB writes a report which is then sent to the Office of the Prosecutor. It is then up to the Prosecutor to accept it or to not accept it. If there's insufficient element -- elements, it can be returned for amendment or it could be rejected altogether. I'm not a lawyer by profession, but I know that that was the practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we move into private session for the next question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to clarify an issue that was raised by Mr. Hannis just before the break; namely, the purpose for which these notes are being sought admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that they cannot and should not be admitted as statements proper for the simple reason that they do not fulfil the requirements of 92 bis. But we will admit them as what they appear to be, namely, as official notes. And so we will consider not only the procedure that these notes seem to establish but also the contents of the findings that were made by the interrogators. As for the weight which we will give to the contents, that, as usually is the case, will remain a task for the Trial Chamber at the end of the trial. So this is just to clarify that we will consider these Official Notes, both for the form and for the contents, and, thus, not consider them as statements. But we can only do so for those notes that have not been signed by the detainees. So if one of these, or some of these notes, appear to have a signature by which the interviewee, or the detainee, has put his signature, then we would say that these would, by virtue of the signature, appear as statements, and that is exactly what we do not wish to admit. So we will only consider those Official Notes that appear as nothing but Official Notes; that is to say, without any signature by the detainee. Those notes which have a signature, and, thus, could be understood to be statements, in our view, would not fulfil the requirements of 92 bis and, therefore, will not be considered. Is that clear? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And should I add, as I was just reminded by the Presiding Judge, that we're not inclined to admit all of these Official Notes but a small representative sample, a small number of them that show sort of -- the pattern in them we will accept. I'm not sure of how many are included in the two exhibits that we have admitted so far, that is to say, 2D122, and 2D123, but I understand it's a limited number and we should just, you know, keep it limited. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm sorry, I wasn't -- I wasn't clear. So is it the Trial Chamber's position that you're going accept some of these Official Notes and not only for the fact that these Official Notes were taken but for the content; is that correct? For the truth of the contents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Not necessarily for the truth. But we will consider the contents. We're not saying that we will establish that this was the truth, but we will consider the evidence that they contain and we will give whatever weight needs to be given to them at the end of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So this is evidence, in our view. We will not necessarily accept this as the truth, but it is important evidence for the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I have a question then. Because as I understood part of what you said earlier was that if it has a signature of a detainee, you're not going to take that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if it has a signature of under the blank that says authorised official you will accept that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But not as a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not as a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's an Official Note with a certain content.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And in terms of authenticity, will you require some evidence about whose signature that is and whether he or she was actually an official at the time; and whether or not this was an official document that was submitted or merely a draft?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I guess those are all arguments that go to weight. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, just in response to your question of whether we will accept the authenticity of these documents, the Chamber's view is that we don't think we need that. We will consider the evidence and give the weight that we find appropriate to it. Already at this point --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, authenticity is always going to be an element of probative value, and I think you're always going have to consider whether documents presented by either side are authentic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- before you can give them any weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- this witness, Mr. Hannis, this witness who we have here has already provided evidence that goes to show that there were indeed notes taken by this or that member of the team and that would seem to us to suffice.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, for the ones where he indicated he recognised the -- the official. I think the last two he was shown he said that's -- that's not a signature. That's an initial. And the other one he said, I don't recognise that signature. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Does that mean that you're challenging the authenticity of those two, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If they're going to be offered for the truth of the contents of those documents, yes we are. Because we don't know who prepared them or when. To the extent that this witness can say, yes, I recognise this signature of a member my team and he was working with me at the time, then, yes. I'm -- that's sufficient authenticity. But if he looks at one and says, I don't know who that is, then we do challenge it. But maybe -- maybe you still accept it but to give it less weight because you're not certain who it was and when it was written.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. Hannis, this is only a suggestion, having regard to what Judge Harhoff has already indicated to Mr. Krgovic that he would select those on which he wishes -- that he finds useful, he may wish to explore those where the witness is unable to identify the signature, that may be the answer to the possible problem that you raise. And as for distinction between an initial and a signature, I -- I don't know that, for evidential purpose, there is any such distinction that we need to concern ourselves with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't want to take any more time with the witness here. We may submit something in writing, if we feel it necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And, Mr. Krgovic, if you understood all of that, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, I just wanted to show some examples. And in my examination so far I haven't shown one where the -- a signature of the person who was interviewed. I just have one or two more. And as for the document which was marked for identification yesterday, I would like to remind the Bench that in previous cases when we discussed the criminal complaint again the Mice and the one relating to Koricanske Stijena and the one Vrbas, we showed some documents because that all goes to show the procedure that was in place. So Koricanska Stijena and the murder at Vrbas and all other cases where the relevant documents contain such Official Notes. That was not contentious when the OTP led such evidence. Now that we are tendering such documents for the same purpose, then, suddenly, that becomes contentious. This would be an observation of mine expressing my attitude, but I will no longer -- I will take no more of the Trial Chamber's time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, speaking about these Official Notes and the information contained therein, at the regular meetings that you had in the morning hours at the SJB of Prijedor, you basically informed Mr. Drljaca about your work, and certainly he had this -- Official Notes in front of him. These notes were sent to him as well as the reports on the interviews conducted; correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Official Notes and other documents were successively sent from the Omarska investigation centre to the Prijedor SJB, and the officer was acquainted with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Speaking about the assessment of your work, that is, the body to which you belonged to, if your immediate superior were to audit your work, he would proceed based on these Official Notes and other documents gathered during the process; correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you confirmed in your earlier evidence that, during the interrogation process, at least as far as people on your team were concerned, that all the laws and regulations were abided by and that these Official Notes were drafted in accordance with the rules and regulations in force; correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: By reviewing this large number of documents and Official Notes, it was possible to establish what you did and how you went about it; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you, in the examination-in-chief, about the list of persons to be brought in for interviews at the Omarska investigation centre. Do you remember the Prosecutor's question to that effect?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the persons who we suggested to Chief Drljaca?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. During the day, analysing these Official Notes, we identified a number of persons who were interesting from the security point of view. There were suggestions made by the operatives, and we forwarded them to the chief of the SJB of Prijedor. He entered them in his diary, work diary. And once the persons were found, they were taken to the investigation centre but for the exclusive purpose of interviewing them in order to corroborate the information that we had collected so far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So the purpose of drafting that list was to establish whether or not some persons could be suspected of taking part in armed rebellion or supporting it, and -- not only due to the fact that they were reputed persons in Prijedor and the surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The suggestion drafted by our team had that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Among those persons, and I'm not going to show you the document again, were individuals from Prijedor itself who were suspected of supporting the rebellion or of providing information to the attackers on Hambarine and Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the majority of the cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness now please be shown Exhibit P1560, 1-5-6-0.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the Prosecutor showed you this document yesterday. And could you please look carefully at item 5 of this document. You said that you hadn't seen this document before, that is to say, in 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't have an opportunity to see it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please zoom in on item 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is the document shown to you by the Prosecutor as well as by Mr. Zecevic. And it says that: "... investigated persons shall be escorted together with the relevant reports to the remand prison in Banja Luka or Stara Gradiska for further criminal processing." You confirmed earlier that you don't know that anyone was taken to Gradiska and that only one person was placed in custody?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about Gradiska. As for Banja Luka, there was one person in detention there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But to your knowledge it wasn't you who sent those people to Gradiska or Banja Luka. Rather, after the processing procedure was completed, they went to Manjaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And now, look at item 4. It says that you were working from 0 to 24, which is virtually around the clock. That's not what you said. You said that sometimes you worked overtime; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have page 3 on this document. Can you please zoom in on item 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed and read out to you item 17, which says that: "The supervision or the implementation of this order shall be supervised by police chief Dusan Jankovic in collaboration with the Banja Luka Security Services Centre." And when asked by the Prosecutor about this, you confirmed that this is right. However, you did not have any contacts with Dusan Jankovic, he did not co-ordinate your work, and he never came to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, I had no contacts with him and he never came to the Omarska centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you know nothing about him performing any co-ordinating work in compliance with this order?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And, finally, sir, the job that you did at Omarska, was not basically regular work that your service carried out.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And your work and the existence of the Omarska investigation centre resulted from a large number of armed conflict and a large number of people brought in in relation to these armed conflicts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were armed clashes and a large number of people were involved in that. But also brought in were people for whom there wasn't such kind of information available.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you established that in the course of screening and interrogation.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. We didn't know the facts at the beginning, so we did it through the interrogation process.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So basically that was the purpose of your job, to establish the truth and the truthful situation, and to establish the status of the people who were brought to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'd like to start with one of the first questions that -- or one of the last questions that Mr. Krgovic put to you with regard to Dusan Jankovic. On the first day of your testimony here, you stated that you were aware that Dusan Jankovic was appointed co-ordinator in the implementation of the order establishing Omarska camp --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Objection. That's not what witness say. And it's leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It's not leading, and it -- if you -- it is what he said, but I'll get to the point of my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were you aware that Dusan Jankovic was the co-ordinator for the implementation of -- the co-ordination and implementation of Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that Dusan Jankovic was Simo's deputy. However, as to the specific job that he was assigned to at that point in time, when Omarska began its work, I knew nothing about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Just to clarify, did you hear from anyone while you were working at Omarska camp that Dusan Jankovic had some role as far as co-ordinating the work at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally heard nothing to that effect. I honestly cannot remember any conversations about Jankovic. Because, basically, throughout the whole period, I only communicated with Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have, what has been marked for identification, 2D123 on the screen? And if we could just turn to the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This is one of the Official Notes that you were shown by Mr. Krgovic. If you can look at the lower right-hand corner, the signatures at the bottom, do you recognise either of those signatures?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot give you the full names of the operatives. But these are the signatures, and the content of this Official Note indicates that these were the interrogators who worked at the investigation centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I understand that. My question is: Do you recognise those signatures? Do you personally recognise whose signatures those belong to?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if I say I do, I should give you their full names, but I can't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can just turn to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This Official Note mentions the name Asim Dergic. Do you recall whether he was at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the family name of Dergic is common in the area the Prijedor. There are quite a few people with that name. I did not know Asim personally, but there were a few Dergics at Omarska investigation centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yesterday you were asked a few questions about the date when Omarska camp began operating, and I want to see if I can clarify this a bit more. At some point, did you have to take another route or detour to get to Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That happened immediately after the attack on Prijedor. I think the attack was carried on the 30th of May, if I'm not mistaken. Later on, at around 10.00 or 11.00, we took another route which is a local road that leads to the Tomasica mine which is also part of the Ljubija mines, i.e., Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And before then, before the 30th of May, did you take the main road to get to Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You were asked yesterday by Mr. Zecevic whether the preliminary interviews of Omarska detainees were based on intelligence that these individuals had been involved in the commission of crimes. On your first day of testimony, you told us that one of your complaints about the arrests of detainees was that the police were bringing them to the camp without any documentation; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were cases of that nature. And that is exactly why we set up this third group, because we thought that these people should be released and set free to go home.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now whether there were two operatives from the SJB working together, I -- I can't confirm with any degree of certainty, although it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yesterday Mr. Zecevic asked you whether all detainees at Omarska were interrogated by the interrogation teams, to which, if I understand it correctly, you said that was the case. Can you tell us how do you know that you interrogated each and every detainee that was held at the camp?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, our task was to conduct interviews with all the people who were brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that. But did you ever go down to the detention rooms and physically check, do a roll-call, to make sure that you have, in fact, interrogated every one at that camp?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a roll-call, and the detainees were brought in to offices for interrogations. And also roll-call was made at the time when they were transported to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, and I don't think you're understanding my question. My question is: Did you -- did the inspection teams or the investigative teams, did they -- to make sure that they've interrogated each and every detainee at the camp, did they participate in the roll-calls or go to the rooms and make sure that they had, in fact, interrogated every single detainee at the camp? Did they perform any checks like that?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometimes a person would be called, his name would be called, but he wasn't there at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could have 1D04-3484 on the screen.

utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, it would be of assistance if we could get a tab number.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I'll note that this is actually a document that's contained within MFI'd Exhibit 2D122. However, it has an English translation, so I'll use this one so that we can follow along.
