utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe the witness has it in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Oh. Well, this may be just easier if I just hand it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday, in response to questions by Mr. Krgovic, you identified three of the alleged perpetrators in this case, this case against Muhamed Cehajic and others, who you personally recalled as being detainees at Omarska and I just want to confirm who they are. First of all, number 3, Esef Crnkic; number 4, Husein Crnkic; and number 11, Muhamed Cehajic. And you also, I think in responses to one of my questions, stated you recall seeing number 12, Becir Medunjanin, at Omarska camp. Sir, if you can just take a quick look at the other names, can you tell us whether you are certain whether any of these other persons were at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am positive about the four, but it is possible that some others were there, but I cannot confirm that because I don't know them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. And we can see that under I think all -- almost all of them that we haven't mentioned, it says that they are currently at large. So we don't know if they were ever, in fact, arrested; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were instances like that. For example, number 1, Mirza Mujagic was not brought there at all because he was on the run at the time. He was the president of the municipal branch -- or the Municipal Board of the Party for Democratic Action in Prijedor. He was not arrested and therefore could not have been brought to the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, perhaps I should tender this into evidence since he has now talked about it. I know it is part of the other document, but we have a translation here and just for clarity's sake may I seek to admit this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I thought -- hold on a minute, Mr. Zecevic. I thought that you were opposed to admitting these notes or documents, but in any case it seems to me that it is already within the package that is contained in 1D -- 2D122. So it's already there. So why do we need to have it admitted once again?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: That's fine. I just wanted it for cross-referencing purposes, but I trust that Your Honours will be able to do that at the end of the day. I will note -- and I apologise I usually provide the title of the document that I'm showing him. This one's entitled: "Decision to Conduct Investigation," dated 5 June 1992. It's by the lower court of Prijedor. It is not an Official Note. It's not a witness statement. It is actually a court document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course, I do not object because that document was in my binder and I decided not to use it because the Trial Chamber took the position based on the objections from the Office of the Prosecutor of yesterday. Now we see that they are changing their position. But nonetheless, I think that I wanted to intervene because I think that the witness with his last question, it wasn't properly -- probably interpreted to the witness. I believe the witness didn't understand the focus of the question of my learned friend. Maybe it should be repeated again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may clarify. Yeah, the document says that the -- some of these people that the witness confirms have been in Omarska, in this document dated 5th of June, it says that these people that the witness confirmed were in Omarska were at large, according to the -- according to this document. And that is the part which I don't think the witness understood. Maybe that should be clarified with the witness. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, I think from his answer it seemed like he did understand the question, but I guess can I ask it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, we were talking about the other 12 persons listed in this decision to conduct an investigation, and we were noting that a significant number of them state that they are -- these perpetrators or alleged perpetrators are currently at large. And my question to you is, so we do not know, in fact, whether these persons were ever arrested or detained; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that for sure, Mirza Mujagic was not apprehended nor brought to the investigation centre. I know that for sure. And I also know for sure that these four were at the investigation centre. As for the rest, I said it is possible that they were there, but I cannot confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Very good. Let's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, I don't know how much longer you intend to be, but I intend to take a break at noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I think I have about ten more minutes. Perhaps we should just break. I note that the next witness we're going to have to do voice distortion, so there is going to be a 20 minute delay before the next witness as well, but I think I have only about -- yeah, I would say ten minutes left. 15 at most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we'll take the break. 20 -- thanks. 20 minutes though. We will try 20 minutes. And, again, could the witness be escorted out first, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. Just that the record shows that Stanisic Defence has been joined by our intern, Jessica Lacey. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So noted, Mr. Zecevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, you may continue, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May we have Exhibit 2D122, marked for identification, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, this is the case file in the Muhamed Cehajic case that Mr. Krgovic had shown you earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can please turn to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, we don't have an English translation, so perhaps you can help me out. I believe this is a request to initiate an investigation sent by the Prijedor Public Prosecutor the lower court in Prijedor on 4 June 1992.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we see under number 3 and number 4, two of the alleged perpetrators that you recall were detained at Omarska, Esef Crnkic and Husein Crnkic. Sir, right to the left of their names there is some handwriting, there is a handwritten word. Can you tell us what is written there?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "died." Both under 3 and under 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could turn to page 4. And if we can look at number 12 --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see another of the alleged perpetrators that you recall was detained at Omarska, Becir Medunjanin. And we also see the same word written to the left of his name as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, if the purpose of this exercise is what I'm -- what I understand it is, Mr. Olmsted and all of us should be aware that this is a case file, so maybe these notes were -- were added in 2002, for example. That is the purpose of my observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's a useful observation but it doesn't prohibit or inhibit the question, line of questioning, Mr. Olmsted is pursuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, but I was just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thanks for the clarification, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, I would consider it more of a piece of evidence than an observation. But, anyway --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: My question is, sir, did you know whether these three Omarska detainees died? Were you aware that they died?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally was not aware of the fact that they died. I know that they were there, but I didn't know of their death. But I have mentioned what happened with regard to one inspector. So I don't rule out the possibility that he acted the same way even earlier. I can't prove that. I do have evidence for the latter case, though. It is possible that he behaved in the same way even before that instance when I observed him committing inhumane acts and violating the law as well as going beyond his legal powers and authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 55 of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Witness, were you able to recognise the handwriting of those additions that had been made to the criminal file that we have just seen, now it's no longer on the screen, but the word "died" apparently was written by someone. Do you know who wrote it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really cannot tell based on that handwriting who wrote it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You were shown this -- I suppose we've agreed on the term Official Note earlier today. And it pertains to a person by the name of Ibrahim Denic. Do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the man personally, but Denic is also a common name at Kozarac. But I have no particular information about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Did you know of a former police officer by that name?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one by the name of Denic, but I forget his given name.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing this police officer, Denic, that you do recall at Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be sure of that, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see in the upper right-hand corner there's something handwritten. Can you tell us what it says?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "got killed."

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recognise the handwriting?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't. I was in no position to watch the colleagues from public security write anything. We were separate before this investigation centre was set up, and we really couldn't watch each other drafting notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yesterday, in the context of Mr. Zecevic's questions regarding first-category detainees, you mentioned Sead Cirkin. Do you know for certain whether Mr. Cirkin was detained at Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military did that. It was Lieutenant-Colonel Majstorovic who started processing that category. Whether the person involved was Cirkin or somebody else, I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to clarify your answer. If I understand you correctly, you don't know for certain whether Sead Cirkin was Omarska camp, detained at Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said that I'm not sure. It is possible that he was there though. The family name of Cirkin is also rather common. So I do know the name of Cirkin, but whether the military was processed -- or, rather, whether the military processed Sead Cirkin, I don't know. An investigation was conducted in Kozarac, and we found out that he -- his task was to organise the military component, that is, to establish platoons, companies, detachments. This is the intelligence collected by the investigation centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, yesterday you told us -- and I'm referring to the beginning of your investigations, in general, yours and your colleagues' investigations in Omarska. You are confronted with a number of people brought in and you have to investigate on them. And it was put to you, and you answered to the positive, that: There was, at the beginning, intelligence about these people's involvement in criminal activities, armed rebellion or whatever, and that your mission was to confirm that there were good grounds for these suspicion or to establish that there were no grounds. You remember -- you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Today, we came back to this issue on, I think, two or three occasions, and at one occasion you said: "There were armed clashes and a large number of people were involved in that but also brought there were people for whom there wasn't such a kind of information available." And then you had to establish whether or not, in the course of your investigation. Now my question is -- and you also said that you often had no documentation at the beginning of -- on why people were brought in. Now my specific question is: At the beginning of the investigation, at the beginning of your interview with a certain detainee, did you have specific information, intelligence on that detainee, and on why he was brought in?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean Sead Cirkin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, I mean in general. I mean in general. At the beginning of your investigation, at the beginning of your interview of each detainee, you and your colleagues, did you have any intelligence on that person, or did you have to establish it during the interview?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was such information, and that was actually the foundation, or, rather, the grounds for us to launch investigations. We wanted to disrupt their activities. Most times the information was about the illegal arming of the population. There was illegal trade in automatic rifles, hand-grenades. Warehouses were built. Large quantities of fuel and food were stored in the area round Kozarac, which all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, my question is, did you have intelligence about this -- about every specific detainee about this? If you say arms, did you have intelligence that this detain that you -- that you were going to interview was suspected to be involved in arm trafficking or in whatever, or was it a general intelligence about things happening and then you trying to establish who of all the people that were brought in were, indeed, involved in these activities?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the persons who had already been taken to the Prijedor SJB before the investigation centre was established - Keraterm and Omarska, that is - there was such information and based on that they were brought in. Later, once the investigation centres were set up, a larger number of people were brought in for whom there was no such information available and that is why we screened them and set up category 3. And our position was, as I have already stated, that these persons should be sent home. But those for whom the suspicion was corroborated were kept and then our work consisted in documenting and processing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I have another question for you, but it has nothing to do with Omarska, so I would perhaps ask you that afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Mr. Witness, do you recall exactly who ordered the interrogations to be commenced at Keraterm and Omarska? On whose orders was this system of interrogation teams set up; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, I really didn't know. I had no such information. Later on, I learned from the media, that is, Dr. Stakic, spoke about it on TV. He was the president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor at the time. And he said then that it was the decision of the Prijedor Crisis Staff. That's the version I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So in your understanding it was the Crisis Staff that had ordered the interrogation of detainees at Keraterm and Omarska and who had also decided how these teams should be composed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was us to determined the composition of the teams, but they made the decisions -- the decisions that applied to the public and had this military aspect and -- and so on. That's what I assume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Just to be sure, I think you have already testified about how the teams were composed, but you said that you decided that yourself. Could you just briefly repeat to me how each team was composed?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the investigation centre was established, we agreed that we should have mixed teams. And as for engaging both services, that decision was taken by another body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So, in the end, there was one from the MUP and one from the army, and the third one was from where?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From state. That is, state security; then there was also public security; and there was military security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. What exactly did you understand to be the purpose of these interrogations? What was the information that you were required to elicit from the detainees?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can honestly say that my understanding was that the purpose was to investigate criminal activities. That is, to establish which persons had been acting illegally. Whether it was about procuring weapons for which no licence could be given, and these are long-barrelled weapons such as automatic rifles and others, so it was my belief that the purpose was to prevent such activity, which was contrary to laws and regulations. That is why we decided that all persons for whom there was no such information should be sent home. But then there was the order of Chief Drljaca that nobody must be released without his approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'll get to that in just a minute. But let me return to what you perceived as the task that you were given. You -- you say that the purpose was to establish whether persons had been acting illegally. Now, that's a very wide notion. Illegal activity could also be theft, or tax fraud, or something other. So my question is to you now: Do you mean to say that the illegal activity was related to the armed conflict, that you were asked to elicit information regarding the activities of the detainees related to the armed conflict? Was that the purpose of your investigation centre?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Illegal arming, which would result in armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And was it your understanding that, as a result of your interrogation, the findings that you made were then to be used in a subsequent judicial prosecution of these people for armed rebellion? Was that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And which, if I may be more specific, which activities did you perceive to be associated with the armed rebellion? You have mentioned procurement of arms. Can you provide us with further detail about which particular activities you, as the interrogation teams, had associated with the armed conflict? What exactly were you looking for?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had intelligence that the population were procuring large quantities of food. They also procured tanker trucks and built stockpiles of fuel. We had information that in the area around Kozarac, some units were being established, from squad, to company, and that persons had been appointed to command these units. Check-points had been set up by these persons, although the police -- it was the police's task to set up check-points where they deemed them necessary. We also had intelligence as to where the medical service would be, or the quartermaster services, if there should be larger conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And who had gathered this intelligence? Where did it come from?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said already that I had already retired in 1991. Until May 1992, I was informed by my colleagues that my service and the Public Security Service, as well as the Military Security Service, had collected such intelligence. What I'm saying I heard from my colleagues during the period when I started working again and later on, when Mr. Vojin Bera presented part of that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Was the information offered to you in writing, or was it given orally?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Tell us exactly how -- how this was given. Was that during the meetings that you had every morning that there would be someone from state security or from the military security intelligence who would provide you with information that, for instance, food-stocks were being gathered or fuel collected or check-points set up? How were you given, and by whom were you given, this information?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially it happened through conversations with my colleagues. However, the investigation confirmed quite a few pieces of information of that kind. For example, people came up with information saying that large quantities of food were being stored, that people were procuring tanker lorries for fuel, et cetera. So people confirmed these facts through investigations. And as for this second part, there were no meetings in the sense that the military security inspector would inform me about their intelligence or someone from the Public Security Service. I did talk to Mijic and I received some information from him though, because he was an active-duty employee in the service and was working both in 1991 and continued thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, my question lies in extension of the question that was put to you by His Honour Judge Delvoie just a while ago. And Judge Delvoie asked you whether you would have in front of you at every occasion where a new detainee was brought into the office where you were conducting the interrogation, whether at each and every such occasion you would have in front of you some documentation that would enable you to interrogate the detainee, and I think you said that you had such file on each and every person that was brought to you. Is that correct, or did I misunderstand?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't have them for all individuals. That particular pertains to the group of people who had been brought in before I was mobilised. They were kept in custody at the SJB, and based on the information available they were arrested. As for the others, quite a few of those who were taken first to Keraterm and then to Omarska, there were no documents accompanying them. These documents were produced in the course of the investigation. The investigation showed that the majority of people had been brought without any information or valid reasons, and, therefore, our view was that these should be sent home. And this is what we started doing at the beginning, but after that, Mr. Drljaca issued this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. But just to be sure, that, for those on whom no file existed, you only had the oral information that was given to you by the intelligence services of the MUP and of the army prior to your interrogation of a detainee. So that was the only basis that you had when you started the interrogation was some oral information given to you by an intelligence officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And were there instances then in which you did not even have this oral information from an intelligence officer from the army or from the MUP; that is to say, were there instances where you had absolutely nothing when the detainee was brought before you?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such instances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During these morning briefings at Mr. Simo Drljaca's office, I would express my opinion that people should not be sent to the investigation centre without proper documentation. Or, if that happens, that such an individual should be accompanied by a file containing the information relating to illegal activities performed by that individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And I understand that Mr. Drljaca then, at some point, opposed -- was opposed to releasing anyone from Omarska or Keraterm. So that brings me back to my question: What did you do in practice when a detainee was brought to you in your office in the interrogation room and you had no information about who this person was or what he was suspected of having doing? What did you do in practice?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would conduct this preliminary interview, let's say. So if this person said nothing that was of interest, or if there was no information acquired from other persons that we had already processed, then this category of people would be the individuals that we requested to be sent home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What were the questions that you would put to him?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we asked them mainly about this activity. Most often we would work on the premise that there was illegal arming of the population. Then he would be asked if, in the area where he lived, there were any paramilitary formations and units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And if the person denied knowledge of any such activity, your recommendation then was that he should be released; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Are you able to give an estimation, just roughly, of how many people out of the hundreds of persons that you interrogated personally, just about how many ended up in that category? I'm just talking about the persons that you interrogated. And I take it from what you have already testified that you must have had at least a couple of hundred interrogations during the time that you were at Omarska. So out of those persons that you interrogated, how many did you recommend belonged to the group that should be sent home? Just roughly.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, we recommended category 3 to be released. Because, for them, we did not have any information of security interests, and our position was that they should be released. But somebody decided to return them from Omarska to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. But my question was: Out of the persons that you interrogated personally, was it 30 per cent that ended up in that group, or 50, or 80? I mean, just roughly speaking, how large a percentage of persons ended up with your recommendation that they should be released?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, roughly speaking, 30 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question: Do you know who rounded up and arrested and brought the detainees to Keraterm and Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a specific and accurate answer. I suppose that both the army and the police were involved in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you know how this was done? Was there a plan to arrest particular persons, or was it actions in which, literally, everyone was rounded up and brought in?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were such cases. In view of the conflict that was going on in Hambarine, in Carakovo, and part of Ljubija, they were carrying out the mopping up of the terrain, and, as far as I know, the majority of the Muslim population were picked up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: When you say that "the majority of the Muslim population was picked up," I suppose that this would be, still, under the suspicion that they had taken part in the armed rebellion, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Because war operations were going on up there, a number of police officers were killed in the forests known as Kurevo. And after that the army and the police started mopping up the area in order to pull out the dead and possibly locate people who were hiding in the area, because this is a forested area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. So in those areas, the majority of the Muslim population would have been suspected of having taken part in the armed rebellion. I mean, the term that you're using yourself, "mopping up" would seem to suggest that it was literally everyone around belonging to the Muslim population that would be arrested and brought in because they were believed to have, in some way or other, taken part in the armed rebellion. Do you know if that was the assumption?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think, for the most part, that was the assumption because the groups that attacked Prijedor were trained in this specific area at Kurevo hill, but I do not rule out the possibility that also rounded up were people who, let's say, were innocent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Final question: Were there women and children and elderly among those that were brought to Omarska and Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were women. I don't know about the children. And there were elderly people as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions. Back to Judge Delvoie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have a document on the screen, please, R093-1297, document ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can anyone of the parties assist me? What I'm looking for is the aerial photo of Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We're checking right now. You're not interested in the one that we showed him in his testimony so far, you're looking for a different one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It could very well be that that's the one. I don't know. You showed him one I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think -- if I may be of assistance, I think it was P1696, the aerial photo of the Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's not Omarska; it's Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I think what will suffice is 65 ter Exhibit 3419.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: 3419.45. Well, yes. Yes, okay. That's fine. Thank you. Mr. Witness, I was just wondering whether you could assist the Trial Chamber in understanding the configuration of this site. You recognised the Keraterm camp here or the ...

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is this building here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could we enlarge the big building with the red roof. That one, yes. Okay. Perfect. You recognise it, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What I wanted to ask you is, when, in the morning you -- you worked here for a few days, you told us. So I would like to know when you arrived here in the morning, I suppose you came by the road in front of the -- of the premises. And then my question --

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: My question is where would your car stop, and where would you enter the building? Could you indicate with -- for instance, with a A the place where car stopped, where you got out of your car; and with a B the place where you entered the building? Perhaps we can zoom in a little bit more. Would be easier, I think. No?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. No, no, let it be then. So I see where you came in. So then you passed the weigh-bridge there on the right side of the entrance road, right? You recognise the weigh-bridge?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we would go from here to the left, and then we would enter the compound from the right. Shall I mark it with an arrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mark -- mark it with an A where you would enter the building, please.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is it. I have already marked it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's -- that's the back of the building, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the main road between Prijedor and Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see -- I see the first -- I suppose that was the first marking you made. That is where you put your car, right? Then --

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is where we would enter. We would park our cars within the parameter. This part of the building was an administration building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And where would that be? Where would that be? Where would you park your car?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this part here. So we would enter the building there, where, on the first floor, there was a restaurant and a number of offices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And where -- where -- I -- I -- I'm a little bit lost here. Where is that? Where would you enter the building -- is that -- does the pen work?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entrance, as far as I know, because I was there only for two days --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was either here. But this part of the building was used as an investigation centre, and the rest were production plants.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Maybe the witness should be instructed, around the building, where he says that part of the building was used then to mark with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I first want to know where he entered the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He should be [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is it -- is it -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] -- Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: He should be instructed to draw on the map --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. He should --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- on the monitor, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: He should mark with an A. Oh, A was where he put the car, okay. With a B the place where you entered the building.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was here, so letter B.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Hmm. That's -- so that is at the back side of the building, you're showing.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know very well that this is the administration part of the building. And immediately we would enter from the main road, go to the parking lot, leave our cars there, enter the building, climb the stairs, and go to the first floor, where the cafeteria and where the offices allocated to us were found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. And where were the people held, the detainees. Where were they held? Did you ever go down there because you were working on the first floor as well, I think, didn't you? Where the cafeteria and the offices were.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The detainees were kept in the production part of the facility. That was on the ground floor. Whether there were garages there as well, I don't know, because I really never went there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The garages should be somewhere here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: One -- one last question. You have the big grey roof, which, I suppose, was a production hall. And at the long side of the building, there is a small -- a small and lower part of building. You see that? You see what I mean? A grey roof as well but it is lower than the very large roof.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was your question, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: My first question is whether you see -- whether you see what I mean. Perhaps the usher can give him the paper -- paper copy of the photo. And show the witness this part where -- that I marked with three Xs. So that's the part where I want to ask a question. You show it to the parties for a moment as well, please. So that you know what I'm talking about. So that the small part I marked with three Xs, could you -- could you please put three Xs on that part as well, on -- on the screen so that we know, for the record, what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah, that's the one. Okay. Can you remember whether that part of the building was there in -- when you were working at Keraterm? If you don't, just say so.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot confirm this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. No problem. Thank you very much. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: One last thing, Witness. Could you, on the roof of the big building, put a C where you think your office was, more or less.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand correctly, then the office was below this spot that I marked on the roof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Can you put a C there, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can you put a C there, please.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And one really last question. Where you entered the building and -- to go to your office, did that look as the main entrance of the building?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So I suppose we would be giving this marked copy a C number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit C1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Witness we thank you for being able to, despite your health difficulties, to -- to continue your testimony until -- through to today. We are finally at an end, and we thank you for your assistance to the Tribunal, and you're now released as a witness. And we wish you a safe journey back home, and of course we wish you all the best in terms of your own health improvement. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, I suppose, whereas, as matter of courtesy to the next witness who has been waiting, we should at least see him today. The practical problem is that the time that it takes to set up the microphone, especially, is such that it would be time to adjourn, so ... Does the OTP have a suggestion?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We've been joined by Ms. Pidwell who will be leading him in evidence, so I will let her speak for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, you're correct in that -- it's a small microphone. I'll bend down. Your Honours, the witness has been waiting for a significant amount of the morning, I'm really not -- and he is quite prepared -- he wanted to wait here so -- rather than in his hotel. He is quite prepared to start and just be sworn in now and be released for tomorrow, or, alternatively, we can release him now and he can start and hopefully finish in one sitting, or continuous sitting, tomorrow. We're really in your hands. I do have a couple of procedural issues that I can fill five minutes with at this juncture, if that assists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: For purely practical purposes, we would request that VWS convey the explanation to him as to why he can't begin until tomorrow. Ms. Pidwell, I assume the matters that you wish to raise should be heard in open court. So we would raise the shutters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, just firstly the Prosecution filed a motion on the 28th of September of this year requesting a subpoena for a particular witness, who I won't name, but we're seeking leave to withdraw that motion and indicating that we would no longer be calling that witness. So we seek leave to take him off our 65 ter witness list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Order as prayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: His number is ST-252, for the record. The other matter that I wish to raise, Your Honours, is in light of the uncertainty of the stipulations and in terms of scheduling for the balance of the month of November, currently on the schedule that we have arranged we have some gaps which will need to be filled by witnesses, if Your Honours require, are going to require us to call witnesses that we would propose to be 92 bis. If we're going to require them for cross-examination to attend personally, they would need to be arranged to come in the last two weeks of November and accordingly, we are wanting an indication or a decision on those witnesses as soon as possible, because most of them live in the region, require visas to attend, and therefore we need some lead-in time to make those arrangements. Otherwise, there will be gaps in the last two weeks in November, because of the -- we have essentially run out of witnesses, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Pidwell.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we have a number of problems with this. The -- the -- the Office of the Prosecutor gives us on Thursday the list of the witnesses for next week. We -- we divide between ourselves the preparation for these witnesses. Now, it took me two days to prepare the Witness ST-252 only to be told today on Wednesday, or Thursday, that's today, that the witness will not be coming at all. And that instead of this witness coming on Monday, as it was suggested to us, that he cannot come because of the subpoena problems and that he will be coming next week, early next week. Now we have another -- new witnesses for the next week. I lost two days in order to prepare the other witness. Now I am told that this witness will not be coming at all. And it requires me to -- to work now for -- for another witness and another witness. I mean, we have to know that. That is -- that was the purpose of the -- of the advance notice on Thursday, who are the witnesses for next week. On such a late -- I mean, I understand things can happen. But that -- that the Office of the Prosecutor, after a week, told us only on Thursday that the witness is not coming at all, that they decided to the withdraw the motion, is, I think, puts the Defence in a very awkward situation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, as you say, things happen, unfortunately. That's the reality of trials. And, of course, we would seek to accommodate you as best we are able to in the changing circumstances of trial. So we take the adjournment, to resume tomorrow morning at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
